extracted.intended_audience: comedians, humor critics, and readers interested in comedy ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for judging when jokes about rape (and similar tragedies) are ethically or artistically defensible versus when they function as threats, humiliation, or celebration of violence. Focuses on purpose, context, power, and effect in stand-up comedy settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor as coping or reclamation
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes about tragedy can be cathartic and empowering; they can help you reclaim control when you’ve lost something or have been damaged beyond repair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author’s example: her own 'rape-portage' joke used privately and in close circles to distance herself from pain while never diminishing it. A defensible rape-related joke often aims to help the teller/process trauma or point out absurdity rather than demean others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invitation/celebration vs. joke
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Would it be funny if this girl got gang raped right this moment...?’ — That’s not a joke. It’s an invitation. It’s a celebration of a violent crime, which is itself another violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If wording or framing treats violence as something to be enacted and laughed at, it crosses from comedic commentary into endorsement or celebration of harm and must be judged unacceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punching down vs. punching up (targeting and power dynamics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using humor to cut someone down, remind them of their vulnerability, or emphasize who is in control is an abuse of comedic power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jokes that target individuals (especially vulnerable or less-powerful people) to humiliate them are ethically different from those that critique powerful institutions or use self-directed vulnerability; assess who is the target and the power relationship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reactive anger vs. thoughtful critique (intent and tone)
rubrics_metrics.description: This incident drew attention because Tosh was more than 'just kidding.' He was angry and reactive to a heckler; his remark functioned as a putdown and threat rather than reflective comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether a remark is a considered comedic device probing an issue, or a spur-of-the-moment, angry retort intended to silence or shame — the latter is far less defensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trivialization/stripping the experience of weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Stripping the experience of its weight, of its tragedy, of its crime—treating it as 'no big deal'—diminishes and devalues survivors' experiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a joke acknowledges the gravity of harm or instead minimizes it; minimizing serious harm is an indicator of unethical or poor comedic judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalization/authentication of harmful half-truths
rubrics_metrics.description: When you reiterate these half-truths (e.g., 'there are girls in the world getting raped by like five guys right now'), they authenticate themselves, as if by magic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a joke repeats or normalizes harmful, misleading, or dehumanizing statements that can perpetuate or legitimize violence and stigma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience and context sensitivity (who is present and how it lands)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedians make rape jokes every day, but context matters — this was said to and about an audience member who had just spoken up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for immediate context (audience composition, presence of survivors, whether a remark directly addresses an individual) when judging appropriateness and likely harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verbal assaults must be marked and managed
rubrics_metrics.description: A friend of 'that girl' wrote about the exchange... We must mark these verbal assaults to manage them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a social responsibility to call out and document aggressive or threatening comedic statements so they can be addressed rather than normalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function of the joke: illuminate vs. humiliate
rubrics_metrics.description: There’s a distinction between making a joke to cope or to point out the absurdity of a situation and using humor to humiliate someone who stood up for something she believed in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the joke's function is to illuminate, critique, or help people cope (potentially defensible) versus to shame, silence, or threaten (problematic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate-threat framing increases harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Framing a violent act as happening 'right now' transforms rhetorical hypotheticals into immediate threats and intensifies their harmfulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider temporal framing: hypotheticals that invoke immediate violence against a specific person are more menacing than abstract commentary and are less likely to be protected as mere joking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedian’s accountability: beyond 'just kidding'
rubrics_metrics.description: Labeling a statement as a joke does not absolve the speaker if the content functions as a threat or assertion of power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess accountability: a performer’s retrospective 'I was joking' must be weighed against the actual effect and apparent intent of the remark.
